claims.claim: Le Guin, quoted by a writing coach, says adjectives and adverbs are rich and good and fattening and the main thing is not to overindulge.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft (1998 ed.), quoted by writing coach Ann Kroeker
claims.quote: Adjectives and adverbs are rich and good and fattening.

claims.claim: A workshop blogger reports that Le Guin calls the no-adjective, no-adverb 'Chastity' exercise the only one she has given to all her workshops.
claims.source: 'Would That I Might' (workshop blogger) working Steering the Craft chapter five, Exercise Five 'Chastity'
claims.quote: the only exercise that she has given to all

claims.claim: Simon Guerrier characterises Steering the Craft as focusing on what you put in each sentence rather than on structure.
claims.source: Simon Guerrier (writer and producer), 'Steering the Craft, by Ursula le Guin', Nothing Tra La La
claims.quote: her focus is on what you put in each sentence

claims.claim: Simon Guerrier glosses Le Guin's 'crowding and leaping' chapter as when to provide lots of detail and where to skip through it.
claims.source: Simon Guerrier, 'Steering the Craft, by Ursula le Guin', Nothing Tra La La
claims.quote: when to provide lots of detail and where to skip through it
claims.page: review, list of the book's chapters

claims.claim: Novelist Jo Walton says A Wizard of Earthsea has never a wasted word and that all the words are right.
claims.source: Jo Walton (novelist), ''Bright the hawk's flight in the empty sky': Ursula Le Guin's A Wizard of Earthsea', Tor.com
claims.quote: There's never a wasted word, and all the words are right.

claims.claim: Jo Walton calls A Wizard of Earthsea one of the best books for reading aloud.
claims.quote: This is one of the best books for reading aloud

claims.claim: Jo Walton attributes her memory of the Earthsea map to Le Guin's names rather than to the map's quality.
claims.quote: Le Guin is so wonderful with names

claims.claim: Jo Walton calls A Wizard of Earthsea one of the very few fantasy novels that succeeds in feeling like a legend.
claims.quote: succeeds in feeling like a legend

claims.claim: Le Guin's FAQ, quoted in the comment thread, says a name's pronunciation affects the sound and rhythm of a sentence.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin's FAQ, quoted by commenter '(still) Steve Morrison' on Jo Walton's Tor.com post
claims.quote: it does have an effect on the sound and rhythm

claims.claim: One reader dissents in the comment thread, saying the prose was visibly beautiful but the style left them cold.
claims.source: An anonymous reader comment on Jo Walton's Tor.com post
claims.quote: I could see how beautiful the prose was, but the style

claims.claim: Le Guin defines the crowding-and-leaping problem as what details are included and what omitted.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft chapter 10 'Crowding and Leaping', quoted at length by 'not a lamb', Daily Kos
claims.quote: It has to do with what details are included, what omitted.

claims.claim: Le Guin says there has to be white space around the word and silence around the voice.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft chapter 10, quoted by 'not a lamb', Daily Kos
claims.quote: white space around the word, silence around the voice
claims.page: block quotation of chapter 10, on leaping

claims.claim: Le Guin states that listing is not describing and that only the relevant belongs.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft chapter 10, quoted by 'not a lamb', Daily Kos
claims.quote: Listing is not describing. Only the relevant belongs.
claims.page: block quotation of chapter 10, on leaping

claims.claim: Le Guin glosses crowding as never using ten vague words where two will do and always seeking the exact word.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft chapter 10, quoted by 'not a lamb', Daily Kos
claims.quote: never to use ten vague words where two will do
claims.page: block quotation of chapter 10, on crowding

claims.claim: Le Guin's crowding means keeping the story interconnected with itself, rich with echoes forward and backward.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, Steering the Craft chapter 10, quoted by 'not a lamb', Daily Kos
claims.quote: keeping it interconnected with itself, rich with echoes forward and backward
claims.page: block quotation of chapter 10, on crowding

verdicts.trueWording: Adjectives and adverbs are rich and good and fattening.
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200, raw HTML). Quote exact; the next sentence is 'The main thing is not to overindulge.', attributed on-page to Le Guin, Steering the Craft, and the site is 'Ann Kroeker, Writing Coach'. Every limb holds. Page does not state which edition (1998) the quote is from; the claim sentence does not assert one.

verdicts.trueWording: she points out that it is the only exercise that she has given to all of her workshops
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact in the opening note. Blogger (William May, 'Would That I Might') is working Steering the Craft chapter five, Exercise Five 'Chastity'; his own commentary confirms the exercise forbids adjectives and adverbs ('the forbidden words', 'functions of not having adjectives and adverbs'). Blogger is a reader working the exercises, not a workshop leader, but the claim's report-limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: Rather than start with the structure then fill in the gaps, her focus is on what you put in each sentence
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200) at the given 2026/01 URL; post dated Friday, January 30, 2026, on 'Nothing Tra La La?', 'The blog of writer and producer Simon Guerrier'. Quote exact; the 'rather than on structure' limb is carried by the same sentence's opening clause.

verdicts.trueWording: what she calls “crowding and leaping” — when to provide lots of detail and where to skip through it
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact, and it sits at the end of the sentence listing the book's chapters ('The chapters cover the sound of your writing spoken aloud, punctuation and grammar, ... and what she calls “crowding and leaping”'). All limbs hold.

verdicts.trueWording: There’s never a wasted word, and all the words are right.
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200, reactormag.com, the Tor.com post republished). Quote exact (curly apostrophe on page) in the prose paragraph: 'how gorgeous the prose is. There’s never a wasted word, and all the words are right. It’s like poetry.' By Jo Walton, published October 4, 2011.

verdicts.trueWording: This is one of the best books for reading aloud
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact, in the same prose paragraph, continuing '—I read it aloud several times when my son was of an age to like a chapter at bedtime.' 'This' refers to A Wizard of Earthsea.

verdicts.trueWording: not because it’s an especially good map but because Le Guin is so wonderful with names
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact in the opening paragraph: 'I could draw the map from memory, and the reason for this isn’t because it’s an especially good map but because Le Guin is so wonderful with names—Selidor, Iffish, Havnor...'. Both limbs (memory attributed to names, not map quality) hold.

verdicts.trueWording: It’s also one of the very few fantasy novels that succeeds in feeling like a legend.
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact, second sentence of the opening paragraph. All limbs hold.

verdicts.trueWording: since it does have an effect on the sound and rhythm of a sentence
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200); the wpDiscuz comment thread (26 comments) is present in the served HTML. Comment by '(still) Steve Morrison' introduces it as 'Le Guin’s FAQ agrees with you about pronunciation; this is what she says:' and quotes the FAQ, whose subject is how to pronounce a made-up name. Every limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: I could see how beautiful the prose was, but the style left me cold.
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200), comment thread. Quote exact; the same comment opens 'I found that the ‘legend’ quality worked against the story for me. It took a few weeks of steady perseverance to get through.' — a clear dissent from Walton's praise. Claim limbs all hold. One source-field wrinkle worth recording: the comment is not anonymous, it carries the handle 'PamAdams'.

verdicts.trueWording: It has to do with what details are included, what omitted.
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200, www.dailykos.com, no block). Quote exact inside the block quotation of Steering the Craft chapter 10 by diarist 'not a lamb'; two sentences later 'I call it Crowding and Leaping', so the defines-limb holds.

verdicts.trueWording: There’s got to be white space around the word, silence around the voice.
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact, in the leaping paragraph of the block quotation: 'But leaping is just as important. What you leap over is what you leave out.'

verdicts.trueWording: Listing is not describing. Only the relevant belongs.
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact, immediately following the white-space sentence in the leaping paragraph.

verdicts.trueWording: never to use ten vague words where two will do, always to seek the vivid phrase, the exact word
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact in the crowding paragraph; the second limb is carried by the clause that follows it, 'always to seek the vivid phrase, the exact word'.

verdicts.trueWording: By crowding, I mean keeping the story full ... keeping it interconnected with itself, rich with echoes forward and backward
verdicts.note: Live page (HTTP 200). Quote exact at the close of the crowding paragraph; 'By crowding, I mean' opens the sentence, so the crowding-means limb holds.
